title: Primes Below a Bound
statement:
Given an integer n, return how many prime numbers are strictly less than n.

A prime is an integer greater than 1 whose only positive divisors are 1 and itself. So 0 and 1 are not prime, and 2 is the only even prime.

examples.why: 2, 3, 5, 7, 11. 13 itself is prime but not counted: the bound is exclusive.
Only 0 and 1 are below 2, and neither is prime.

hints: Testing each number by trial division up to its square root works, but does a lot of repeated work for millions of numbers.
Turn it around: instead of asking whether k is prime, let each prime cross out the numbers it divides.
Sieve of Eratosthenes: for each p from 2 while p · p < n, if p is still unmarked, mark p·p, p·p + p, … as composite. Count what stays unmarked.

explain.intuition:
Checking every number on its own repeats the same divisions again and again. The sieve flips the question. Start with every number from 2 to n − 1 marked "maybe prime". Take the smallest unmarked number p: nothing smaller divides it, so it is prime. Cross out all its multiples. Repeat.

Two details make it fast. Crossing out can start at p · p, because any smaller multiple p · q with q < p was already crossed out by q's prime factor. And you can stop once p · p ≥ n, since every composite below n has a factor no bigger than its square root. The total work is about n log log n, which behaves almost like linear.
steps: Create a boolean array composite of size n, all false.
For p from 2 while p · p < n: if composite[p] is false, mark p·p, p·p + p, … below n as composite.
Count the indexes from 2 to n − 1 that are still false.
pitfalls: Counting n itself when it is prime. The bound is strict.
Treating 0 and 1 as prime, or crashing on n = 0 and n = 1 by indexing past a tiny array.
Starting the crossing-out at 2p and stopping only at n. Correct, but it does far more work than needed.

solutions.title: Trial division for every number
solutions.idea: For each k below n, try divisors up to √k.

solutions.title: Sieve of Eratosthenes
solutions.idea: Each prime crosses out its multiples, starting from its square. What is never crossed out is prime.

followups: Return the primes themselves. How much memory does that take for n = 5 000 000?
